extracted.intended_audience: pre-service and in-service middle school mathematics teachers; teacher-educators and course designers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and delivering precalculus and calculus content courses for future middle-school mathematics teachers, with emphasis on vertical connections to school mathematics, collaborative activities, online tools, and assessment. Covers modeling heuristics, vignette use, applet/features, course format, and learning objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling — Explore (critical thinking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore. Critical thinking is incorporated as part of the heuristic, employing either inductive or deductive reasoning, working backwards from subgoals, and visualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the DECAL heuristic used in the course; introduced in the first mathematics session and recalled when putting topics (e.g., finite differences, least squares) into context. Emphasize inductive/deductive reasoning, subgoal decomposition, and visualization as first step of modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling — Create a model
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a model that is relevant to the information and setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate a mathematical representation appropriate to the problem context (connect to data collection and the intended question). This is the second step in the modeling heuristic and should be taught and practiced explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling — Apply the model
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the model to answer the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the created model to produce predictions, computations, or explanations addressing the posed question; include testing against data where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling — Link the model to new situations (conceptual check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Link the model to new situations to provide a conceptual check of its validity and to make sure it answers the original question appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage transferring the model to related contexts as a validity check and to reveal limitations; use earlier analyses (e.g., triangular numbers) to show why similar rules appear across problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use finite differences appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite differences is a useful modeling tool as long as the data collected follow a simple underlying mathematical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer finite differences for combinatorial counting problems (clean data) or problems from physics with little experimental error. It is less useful for noisy data, such as many social-science data sets. Example: edge-counting in complete graphs yields data amenable to finite-difference modeling; Tower of Hanoi gives non-polynomial behavior for contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use least squares (and consider alternative error measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach to minimizing error in a constrained model by the method of least squares is the most sophisticated modeling technique developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use applets (e.g., NCTM Illuminations) to show geometric intuition (squares of errors) and how outliers affect error strongly. Also demonstrate alternate error measures (sum of absolute errors, sum of shortest distances) and let students experiment by dragging points and lines to explore minimization strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vignettes to elicit classroom-relevant discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vignettes (short scenes focusing on one moment) are useful for bringing points into focus from research readings and for sparking discussion in online forums and class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present common classroom misunderstandings as vignettes to elicit discussion, invite in-service and pre-service teachers to share experiences, and rehearse effective teaching strategies. Vignettes also provoke sidebar discussions and deeper exploration via chat or forum without being disruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vignette design: state misconception and prompt diagnosis/remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each vignette pairs a stated misconception with a prompt asking what misconception might exist and how to address it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief, concrete examples (e.g., 'Students believe a number can be both even and odd', or decimal-place-value confusions) and ask students to diagnose the underlying thinking and propose instructional responses. Provide transcripts or exemplar discussions where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and integrate online resources tied to standards and grade bands
rubrics_metrics.description: Curate online resources (e.g., NCTM Illuminations, NLVM, SHODOR, NSDL, Math Forum) that are tied to standards and can be filtered by grade band and subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose resources that align with Connected Mathematics lessons and state standards; make links available on course slides and demonstrate key sites in class. These resources can substitute for physical manipulatives for at-home practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide custom applets with a coherent, stable UI for exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use custom Java applets and graphing utilities to illustrate course points and provide a stable interface for student exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applet features should include parsing algebraic expressions (exponents, logs, trig, inverse trig), color-coded function graphs and tables, coordinate display modes, drag-to-move points/vertices, zoom modes (coordinates, drag-rectangle, zoom buttons), table-by-hand x-entry, and controls to adjust coefficients (arrows or fields). Show how specific applets (e.g., least squares, quadratic explorers) support conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address online-instruction challenges with multiple representations and appropriate tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is difficult to teach online because clear communication depends on symbols, diagrams, and graphical/tabular representations not easily conveyed in audio-only or plain-text chat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model face-to-face teaching by providing multiple ways of understanding a concept (symbolic, graphical, tabular, pictorial), choose conferencing software with audio-visual streaming, application sharing (appsharing), and whiteboards, and allow two-way sharing so students can interact with resources. Encourage discussion boards and small learning communities and provide ample faculty access via email or asynchronous channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course format: activity- and discussion-based guided discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Both courses are activity and discussion based, with the goal of having students learn mathematics through guided discovery, and modeling teaching practices for their classrooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermix short instructor introductions with collaborative small-group activities, pause for large-group discussions when needed, and include informal student presentations. Instructor refrains from lecture-heavy formats and intentionally defers correctness judgment to the class to foster a class-driven sense-making culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework policy: limited, frequent, and broadly graded
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework is assigned at each class meeting, no more than ten problems per class, chosen to provide practice on recently developed concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect a sample of solutions weekly and grade broadly (check / check-minus / zero for correct / partially correct / not done) so the instructor can monitor student understanding without punitive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student journals written for peer audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Students turn in journals with explanations to selected questions of the day and reflections on video case studies and curriculum excerpts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to write their journals thinking of their peers as audience to develop clear explanations and reflective practice useful for teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment structure: written work, mathematical take-home exams, final project
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' grades are based on submitted written work (homework and journals), three take-home exams (strictly mathematical problems), and a final project (two-problem comparison paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make take-home exams mathematically rigorous (some may be phrased in a teaching context) and require the final project to analyze unifying mathematical ideas between college-level and middle-grades problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precalculus learning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Precalculus course goals: develop a firm understanding of the concept of function, analyze functional behavior, and understand covariation (transformations, inverses, solving equations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize multiple representations (verbal, concrete, pictorial, tabular, symbolic, graphical), study exponential, logarithmic, power, polynomial, rational, trigonometric functions and functions not described by a formula, and highlight connections to school mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculus learning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculus course goals: introduce basic concepts of calculus focusing on differentiation and integration and their relationship and applications (rates of change, area under a curve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should explain the derivative as a rate of change and geometrically, use tangent-line approximations, analyze increase/decrease/concavity/extrema, sketch derivative graphs and possible originals given derivative graphs, compute area via Riemann sums and definite integrals, and apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus especially to problems grounded in middle school mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential course elements tying content to middle-school teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Course elements that tie teaching mathematics to middle schoolers: carefully chosen collaborative activities, daily question-of-the-day discussions, inclusion of video case studies, highlighting mathematical connections with middle-school curricula, and the two-problem comparison paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements set the capstone courses apart from standard college offerings by explicitly linking college-level mathematics to K–8 pedagogy and curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design collaborative activities to unpack ideas and surface student thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative activities should be chosen to unpack mathematical ideas, support guided discovery, and reveal connections between middle-school and college-level perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use manipulatives (e.g., patty paper), coordinate-notation translation activities (sailboat example), and tasks that force comparison of geometric and functional viewpoints so pre-service teachers confront and remedy likely student confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vetted activity sources (Teacher Quality Modules, Math in the Middle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary activity sources: Teacher Quality Modules for precalculus activities and Math in the Middle Project worksheets for calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For precalculus, use modules like 'Linking Foundations' and 'Characteristics of Exponentials and Logarithms'; for calculus, use an 18-worksheet sequence moving from limits to integration, roughly one worksheet per week. Instructor introduces context briefly, students work collaboratively, then class discussion identifies the big ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pre/post testing to measure conceptual gains
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ pre- and post-tests to measure improved conceptual understanding resulting from activity-based instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pre/post assessment around logarithms showed improved understanding that a logarithm is an exponent and how logarithm properties follow from exponent properties; use such measures to evaluate effectiveness of chosen activities.
